/treatments/drug-guide.title: Arthritis Medicines Explained: A Plain-English UK Guide | Living With Arthritis
/treatments/drug-guide.description: What each type of arthritis medicine does, from painkillers to DMARDs and biologics, how long they take to work, typical monitoring and what to ask your team.
/treatments/drug-guide.question: Arthritis medicines explained: a plain-English guide
/treatments/drug-guide.answer: Arthritis medicines fall into two broad groups: those that ease symptoms such as pain and stiffness, and those that calm the underlying disease in inflammatory arthritis. Painkillers work within hours; disease-modifying medicines usually take weeks to months. Your rheumatology team or GP will choose and adjust them with you, so never start, stop or change a dose on your own.
/treatments/drug-guide.about: Arthritis medicines explained: a plain-English guide
/treatments/drug-guide.bodyHtml:
Written by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Updated 2026-09-25. Pending clinical review.

Two jobs: easing symptoms and controlling the disease

It helps to sort arthritis medicines by the job they do. Some ease symptoms. Painkillers, anti-inflammatory tablets and gels, and steroid injections all fall into this group. They can make a real difference to how you feel today, but they do not change the long-term course of inflammatory arthritis.

Others control the disease itself. In rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, axial spondyloarthritis, lupus and related conditions, the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. Disease-modifying medicines calm that process and help protect joints and organs from damage over time. They work slowly, which is why people are sometimes given a short course of steroids as a bridge while they wait for them to take effect.

Osteoarthritis is different. There is no medicine that reverses it, so treatment focuses on exercise, weight, footwear and aids, with painkillers used to help you stay active rather than as the main treatment.

Read more: Osteoarthritis vs rheumatoid arthritis · Inflammatory arthritis guide

Painkillers and anti-inflammatories

Paracetamol is widely used, although for osteoarthritis its benefit is often modest. Anti-inflammatory gels rubbed onto a sore knee or hand are a sensible early option for many people, because much less of the medicine reaches the rest of the body than with tablets.

Anti-inflammatory tablets (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen and naproxen can ease pain and stiffness, especially in inflammatory conditions. They can irritate the stomach and affect the kidneys, blood pressure and heart, so they are usually given at the lowest dose that helps, for the shortest time needed, sometimes with a stomach-protecting tablet. Check with a pharmacist before combining them with other medicines, including ones bought over the counter.

Stronger painkillers such as codeine are used cautiously, because they often cause constipation, drowsiness and dependence and tend to help long-term joint pain less than people hope.

Read more: Painkillers and NSAIDs guide · Paracetamol vs ibuprofen · Topical NSAIDs: often overlooked · When you need stomach protection

Steroids

Steroids (corticosteroids) are powerful anti-inflammatories. They can be injected into a joint, given as an injection into muscle, or taken as tablets. They often work quickly, which makes them useful for flares and for bridging the gap before a slower medicine starts working.

Longer courses can raise blood sugar and blood pressure, thin the bones, increase infection risk and affect mood and sleep. If you have taken steroid tablets for more than a few weeks, stopping suddenly can be dangerous, so your team will reduce them gradually. You may be given a steroid emergency card to carry.

Read more: Steroids for arthritis · Steroid injections vs tablets

Conventional DMARDs

Disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) are usually the first long-term treatment for inflammatory arthritis. Methotrexate is the most commonly used. Others include sulfasalazine, leflunomide and hydroxychloroquine, and some people take two or three together.

They typically take several weeks to a few months to reach their full effect. Most need regular blood tests to check your blood count, liver and kidneys, often more frequently at the start. The tests are how your team spots problems early, so it matters to keep the appointments even when you feel well.

Some DMARDs are not suitable around pregnancy, and some interact with alcohol or other medicines. Your team will talk you through what applies to your medicine.

Read more: DMARDs and methotrexate explained · Managing methotrexate side effects · Azathioprine guide · Should you start DMARDs at diagnosis?

Biologics, biosimilars and JAK inhibitors

If conventional DMARDs do not control your disease well enough, your specialist may suggest a targeted treatment. Biologics are injections or drips that block specific signals in the immune system, such as TNF, IL-6, IL-17 or IL-23. Biosimilars are close copies of branded biologics that work in the same way and are widely used in the NHS.

JAK inhibitors are tablets that block signals inside immune cells. They are an option for some people with rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis.

In England and Wales, access to these medicines is guided by NICE, and your specialist will check whether you meet the criteria. Because they dampen parts of the immune system, you will be screened for infections such as tuberculosis beforehand and advised about vaccines.

Read more: DMARDs vs biologics · Biologics: a year-one roadmap · JAK inhibitors explained · How NHS access to biologics works

Medicines for gout, bones and nerve pain

Gout is treated in two ways: medicines to settle a flare, such as colchicine, anti-inflammatories or steroids, and long-term urate-lowering medicines such as allopurinol or febuxostat that stop crystals forming. Urate-lowering treatment is usually started at a low dose and increased gradually, with blood tests to guide the dose.

If you are at risk of osteoporosis, for example after long courses of steroids, you may be offered bone-protecting medicines alongside calcium and vitamin D. For pain that has become widespread or nerve-like, low doses of medicines such as amitriptyline are sometimes used for their effect on pain signals and sleep rather than on mood.

Read more: Gout medication in the UK · Febuxostat for gout · Amitriptyline for pain

Staying safe on long-term medicines

A few habits make long-term treatment safer and easier:

  • Follow the plan your own rheumatology team or GP gives you, and never start, stop or change a dose yourself.
  • Keep your blood-test appointments and know how to reach your rheumatology advice line.
  • Tell every doctor, dentist and pharmacist what you take, including supplements and herbal remedies.
  • Ask what to do if you become unwell with an infection, as some medicines are paused during illness only on your team's advice.
  • Check vaccine advice before any jab, especially live vaccines.
  • Raise pregnancy plans early, whatever your sex, as some medicines need changing months ahead.
  • If you pay for prescriptions in England, look into a prepayment certificate.

Read more: Supplement and medicine interactions · Prescription costs and prepayment certificates · Stopping arthritis medication safely · Talking to your GP about medication worries

Questions worth asking when a new medicine is suggested

It is normal to feel uncertain about a new medicine. Writing questions down before your appointment helps. Useful ones include: what is this for and what should I notice if it is working; how long before I can tell; what side effects should I report and how quickly; which blood tests do I need and how often; can I drink alcohol; what about pregnancy, vaccines and infections; and what happens if it does not work.

The NHS website, the British National Formulary (BNF) patient information and the leaflet in your medicine box are all reliable places to read more.

faqs.q: How long do arthritis medicines take to work?
faqs.a: Painkillers and anti-inflammatories usually help within hours. Steroid injections often help within days. DMARDs, biologics and JAK inhibitors typically take weeks to a few months to reach their full effect, so your team will usually review you after a set period before deciding whether it is working.

faqs.q: Why do I need blood tests on some arthritis medicines?
faqs.a: Several disease-modifying medicines can affect your blood count, liver or kidneys, often without symptoms at first. Regular tests let your team spot changes early and adjust treatment safely. The schedule depends on the medicine and how long you have been taking it.

faqs.q: Can I stop my medicine if I feel better?
faqs.a: Please do not stop without talking to your rheumatology team or GP. Feeling better often means the medicine is working. Stopping suddenly can trigger a flare, and stopping steroids suddenly can be dangerous. Some people can reduce treatment later, but only with a planned approach agreed with their team.

faqs.q: Is it safe to take supplements with arthritis medicines?
faqs.a: Some supplements interact with arthritis medicines or affect the liver or bleeding. Always tell your pharmacist and rheumatology team before starting a supplement or herbal remedy, and bring the packet with you if you are unsure what it contains.

faqs.q: What should I do if I get an infection while on a DMARD or biologic?
faqs.a: Contact your GP or rheumatology advice line promptly and tell them what you take. Some medicines are paused during an infection, but only on professional advice. Seek urgent help for high fever, breathlessness, confusion or feeling very unwell.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay for arthritis prescriptions?
faqs.a: Prescriptions are free in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. In England, charges apply unless you are exempt, for example because of age or certain benefits. A prescription prepayment certificate can reduce the cost if you need several items regularly.

/treatments/surgery-options.title: Arthritis Surgery Options: Keyhole to Joint Replacement | Living With Arthritis
/treatments/surgery-options.description: An overview of arthritis operations in the UK, from arthroscopy and fusion to joint replacement: who they help, recovery times and what to ask your surgeon.
/treatments/surgery-options.question: Arthritis surgery options: from keyhole to joint replacement
/treatments/surgery-options.answer: Surgery is usually considered when arthritis pain or stiffness is seriously limiting your life and non-surgical treatment has been tried properly. Joint replacement is the most common operation, but fusion, realignment and smaller procedures also have a place. The right choice depends on the joint, your symptoms, your health and what matters most to you.
/treatments/surgery-options.about: Arthritis surgery options: from keyhole to joint replacement
/treatments/surgery-options.bodyHtml:
Written by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Updated 2026-09-25. Pending clinical review.

When is surgery worth considering?

Most people with arthritis never need an operation. Exercise, weight management, pain relief, physiotherapy, aids and, for inflammatory arthritis, disease-modifying medicines help the majority. Surgery comes into the conversation when pain disturbs your sleep most nights, when your walking distance or hand use has shrunk to the point that daily life is hard, or when a joint is visibly changing shape despite good treatment.

X-ray appearance alone does not decide it. Two people with similar X-rays can have very different symptoms. The key questions are how much the joint is affecting your life, what you have already tried, and whether the likely benefits outweigh the risks for you.

Read more: How do I know if surgery is right for me? · Is it too soon for a joint replacement? · Physiotherapy vs surgery for knee arthritis

Joint replacement

In a joint replacement (arthroplasty), the worn surfaces of the joint are removed and replaced with metal, plastic or ceramic parts. Hip and knee replacements are the most common and, for the right person, can ease pain dramatically and restore walking. Shoulder, elbow, ankle and finger joints can also be replaced, although these operations are done less often and in more specialised centres.

Some people with arthritis in only one part of the knee are suitable for a partial knee replacement, which keeps more of their own joint. Your surgeon will explain which type suits your joint and why.

Read more: Total knee replacement: a UK patient's guide · Knee replacement surgery guide · Hip replacement recovery week by week · Hip replacement and arthritis

Joint fusion

Fusion (arthrodesis) joins the bones of a painful joint so that it no longer moves. That sounds drastic, but in joints where a little movement matters less than being pain-free and stable, such as some joints in the ankle, foot, wrist, thumb or fingers, fusion can work very well and last a long time.

The trade-off is lost movement at that joint, which nearby joints partly make up for. Recovery usually involves a period in a cast or boot while the bones knit together.

Read more: Joint fusion vs replacement: how surgeons choose

Realignment, keyhole and other procedures

An osteotomy cuts and realigns a bone to shift weight away from the worn part of a joint. It is sometimes offered to younger, active people with arthritis on one side of the knee, to delay the need for a replacement.

Keyhole surgery (arthroscopy) uses a camera and small instruments. For osteoarthritis of the knee, washing out or tidying the joint is not recommended by NICE as a routine treatment, because it does not help most people more than exercise and other care. It may still be used for specific mechanical problems such as a joint that genuinely locks.

Other operations include removing inflamed joint lining (synovectomy), releasing a trapped nerve, as in carpal tunnel surgery, removing a small wrist bone to relieve thumb-base arthritis (trapeziectomy), and repairing tendons damaged by inflammatory arthritis.

Read more: Knee arthroscopy for osteoarthritis: helpful or hype? · Shoulder arthroscopy and arthritis · Carpal tunnel syndrome

Getting ready for an operation

What you do in the weeks before surgery can make recovery smoother. Strengthening the muscles around the joint, often called prehabilitation, helps you get moving afterwards. Stopping smoking, keeping diabetes and blood pressure well controlled, and treating any skin or dental infections all lower the risk of complications.

Plan your home before you go in: a firm chair of the right height, things you use daily moved to waist height, help with shopping and lifts, and any equipment the occupational therapist recommends. If you take medicines for inflammatory arthritis, ask your rheumatology and surgical teams well ahead whether any need pausing around the operation. Do not stop anything without their advice.

Read more: Prehabilitation before surgery · Help while you wait for treatment

Recovery and risks

Recovery is a process of weeks to months, not days. Most people are helped to get up soon after joint replacement and go home with an exercise plan. Pain, swelling and tiredness are normal early on and gradually settle. Driving, returning to work and getting back to sport each have their own timelines, which your team will guide.

Every operation carries risks, including infection, blood clots, problems with the anaesthetic, nerve or blood vessel injury, ongoing pain, stiffness and, sometimes, the need for further surgery. Your surgeon should talk you through your personal risks, which depend on your health and the procedure.

  • Seek urgent help for calf pain and swelling, chest pain or sudden breathlessness after surgery.
  • Contact the ward or your GP promptly about a wound that becomes red, hot, leaking or increasingly painful, or if you develop a fever.

Questions to ask your surgeon

Before you agree to surgery, ask what the operation involves and what it is likely to achieve for you specifically. Ask what the alternatives are, including not having surgery yet, and what would happen if you waited. Ask about your personal risks, the likely recovery time, when you could drive and work, and what help you will need at home. It is reasonable to ask for time to think and, if you are unsure, a second opinion.

Read more: Is it worth paying for a second opinion?

Related guides

  • Joint replacement surgery
  • Arthritis medicines explained
  • Physiotherapy for arthritis
  • Complementary therapies

faqs.q: Can I have surgery if I have rheumatoid arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes. People with inflammatory arthritis have joint replacements and other operations regularly. Your surgical and rheumatology teams will plan together, including whether any medicines need pausing around the operation, which should only be done on their advice.

faqs.q: Am I too young or too old for a joint replacement?
faqs.a: There is no fixed age limit. Surgeons weigh your symptoms, general health and activity levels. Younger, very active people may need a further operation later in life, so timing is discussed carefully. Being older is not a reason on its own to rule surgery out.

faqs.q: Will I need to lose weight before surgery?
faqs.a: Some surgical teams ask people to work on their weight first, because it can reduce complications and help recovery. Policies vary around the UK. Ask your GP or surgeon what applies to you and what support is available.

faqs.q: Does keyhole surgery help knee osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: For most people with knee osteoarthritis, keyhole washout or tidying of the joint does not help more than exercise and other non-surgical care, and NICE does not recommend it routinely. It may be used for a specific mechanical problem such as true locking.

faqs.q: What can I do while I wait for my operation?
faqs.a: Keep as active as you can, work on strength around the joint, manage pain with your GP or pharmacist, and prepare your home. Tell your GP if things get significantly worse while you wait, as your priority may need reviewing.

faqs.q: How long does a joint replacement last?
faqs.a: Modern hip and knee replacements usually last many years, and most people will not need another operation on the same joint. How long yours lasts depends on factors including your age, activity level and the type of implant. Your surgeon can talk through what to expect.

/treatments/complementary-therapies.title: Complementary Therapies for Arthritis: What Evidence Says | Living With Arthritis
/treatments/complementary-therapies.description: Acupuncture, massage, supplements, tai chi and more: an honest guide to complementary therapies for arthritis, their evidence, costs, safety and interactions.
/treatments/complementary-therapies.question: Complementary therapies for arthritis: what the evidence says
/treatments/complementary-therapies.answer: Some complementary approaches, such as tai chi, yoga, mindfulness and massage, can help people with arthritis feel and move better alongside usual care. Others, including many supplements, have weak or mixed evidence. None should replace medicines prescribed for inflammatory arthritis. Check safety and interactions first, use regulated practitioners, and judge a therapy by whether it helps you do more.
/treatments/complementary-therapies.about: Complementary therapies for arthritis: what the evidence says
/treatments/complementary-therapies.bodyHtml:
Written by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Updated 2026-09-25. Pending clinical review.

Complementary, not alternative

Complementary therapies are used alongside standard treatment. Alternative therapies are used instead of it. For osteoarthritis, trying a gentle complementary approach alongside exercise and pain relief is often reasonable. For inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, replacing disease-modifying medicines with an alternative remedy can allow permanent joint damage, so please do not stop prescribed treatment without talking to your rheumatology team.

Many people try something complementary because they want more control, fewer tablets, or help with stress and sleep. Those are good reasons. The aim of this guide is to help you spend your time and money where it is most likely to help.

How to judge a therapy

A few questions cut through most marketing claims:

  • Has it been tested in fair trials in people with your type of arthritis, not just in a laboratory or in animals?
  • Are the claims modest and specific, or does it promise to cure arthritis or detox your joints?
  • Is the practitioner registered with a recognised regulator or professional body?
  • What does it cost over a full course, and is there a trial period?
  • Could it interact with your medicines or affect bleeding, the liver or blood sugar?
  • After a fair trial, can you do more, such as walk further, sleep better or use your hands more easily?

Movement-based approaches

Tai chi, yoga, Pilates and water-based exercise are among the best-supported options because they combine gentle strengthening, balance and relaxation. They count as exercise, which is a core treatment for osteoarthritis and helps people with inflammatory arthritis too. Classes adapted for arthritis or for older adults are widely available, and many sessions can be done seated.

Read more: Tai chi for arthritis joint pain · Yoga for arthritis · Hydrotherapy and arthritis · Yoga vs Pilates for arthritis

Hands-on therapies

Massage can ease muscle tension and help some people relax and sleep, although effects on joint pain tend to be short-lived. Avoid firm pressure over a hot, swollen joint during a flare.

Osteopaths and chiropractors use manipulation and mobilisation, mainly for back and neck pain. In the UK both professions are regulated by law, so check your practitioner is registered with the General Osteopathic Council or the General Chiropractic Council. High-velocity manipulation of the neck is not suitable for everyone, particularly people with inflammatory arthritis affecting the neck or with osteoporosis, so mention your diagnosis first.

Acupuncture and TENS

Acupuncture involves fine needles placed at specific points. Some people with back or knee pain find it helps for a while. NICE does not recommend acupuncture as a treatment for osteoarthritis, because trials have not shown a meaningful benefit over sham treatment. If you decide to try it, choose a practitioner registered with a recognised professional body and agree a limited number of sessions.

A TENS machine delivers mild electrical pulses through pads on the skin. It is cheap, drug-free and under your control, and some people find it takes the edge off pain. It is not suitable for everyone, for example if you have a pacemaker, so check first.

Read more: Acupuncture library note · TENS machines for arthritis

Supplements and herbal remedies

Supplements are the area where money is most easily wasted. Glucosamine and chondroitin have been studied a lot with mixed results, and NICE does not recommend glucosamine for osteoarthritis. Turmeric (curcumin) and fish oils have some encouraging small studies but are not a substitute for medical treatment. Vitamin D is worth checking if you rarely get outdoors, as low levels are common in the UK.

Natural does not mean harmless. Several herbal products can affect the liver, interact with methotrexate or blood thinners, or change how other medicines work. Supplements are also not regulated as strictly as medicines, so the dose and purity can vary. Tell your pharmacist and rheumatology team before starting anything new.

Read more: Turmeric and curcumin: the evidence · Glucosamine vs collagen · Omega-3 fish oil and arthritis · Vitamin D and arthritis · Supplement and medicine interactions · Turmeric and methotrexate

Mind-body approaches

Long-term pain affects mood, sleep and stress, and each of those can turn the volume of pain up. Mindfulness, relaxation training and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) do not fix joints, but they can change how much pain takes over your life. CBT-based support is available through NHS talking therapies services, and in England you can usually refer yourself.

Read more: Mindfulness for arthritis pain · CBT for chronic pain

Heat, cold and simple home remedies

Warmth, such as a warm bath, a heat pack or a hot water bottle wrapped in a cover, often eases stiffness. Cold packs wrapped in a towel can calm a hot, swollen joint. These are cheap, low-risk and easy to test. Protect your skin, limit each session to around the length recommended on the product, and avoid heat on numb skin.

Read more: Heat vs cold for arthritis pain

Related guides

  • Supplements hub
  • Natural arthritis pain relief
  • Arthritis medicines explained
  • Surgery options

faqs.q: Are complementary therapies available on the NHS?
faqs.a: Some movement-based options such as exercise classes, hydrotherapy and physiotherapy-led programmes are available on the NHS in many areas, and talking therapies are widely available. Most other complementary therapies are paid for privately, and availability varies by area.

faqs.q: Can I use complementary therapies instead of my arthritis medicines?
faqs.a: Not for inflammatory arthritis. Disease-modifying medicines protect your joints from damage that complementary therapies cannot prevent. Use complementary approaches alongside your treatment, and talk to your rheumatology team before changing anything.

faqs.q: Is glucosamine worth taking for osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: The evidence is mixed and NICE does not recommend glucosamine for osteoarthritis. Some people still choose to try it. If you do, tell your pharmacist, check it will not interact with your medicines, and stop if you notice no benefit after a fair trial.

faqs.q: How do I find a safe practitioner?
faqs.a: Check registration: osteopaths and chiropractors must be registered with their statutory regulators, and other therapists should belong to a recognised professional body. Tell them your diagnosis and medicines, and ask about costs and the expected number of sessions up front.

faqs.q: Do copper bracelets or magnets help arthritis?
faqs.a: Trials have not shown copper or magnetic bracelets to be better than dummy bracelets for arthritis pain. They are unlikely to cause harm, but it is worth putting your money towards approaches with better evidence.

faqs.q: How long should I try a therapy before deciding?
faqs.a: Agree a sensible trial in advance, for example a set number of sessions or a few weeks of a supplement, and note how your pain and daily activities change. If you cannot see a clear benefit by the end, it is reasonable to stop.

/guides/work-with-arthritis.title: Working With Arthritis: Rights, Adjustments and Support | Living With Arthritis
/guides/work-with-arthritis.description: A practical UK guide to working with arthritis: your legal rights, telling your employer, reasonable adjustments, Access to Work, flexible working and sick leave.
/guides/work-with-arthritis.question: Working with arthritis: your rights, adjustments and support
/guides/work-with-arthritis.answer: Many people with arthritis keep working, often with changes to how, when or where they do their job. If your arthritis has a substantial, long-term effect on daily life, UK law usually counts it as a disability, which means your employer must consider reasonable adjustments and must not treat you unfairly. Access to Work can help pay for equipment and support.
/guides/work-with-arthritis.about: Working with arthritis: your rights, adjustments and support
/guides/work-with-arthritis.bodyHtml:
Written by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Updated 2026-09-25. Pending clinical review.

Your legal protection at work

In England, Scotland and Wales, the Equality Act 2010 protects disabled people at work. You are likely to count as disabled if your arthritis has a substantial and long-term effect on your ability to do normal daily activities. Long-term usually means it has lasted, or is likely to last, at least 12 months. The effect is judged as if you were not taking treatment, so well-controlled arthritis can still qualify. In Northern Ireland, similar protection comes from the Disability Discrimination Act 1995.

This protection covers recruitment, pay, training, promotion and dismissal. It also puts a duty on employers to make reasonable adjustments so you are not at a disadvantage because of your condition.

Read more: Your workplace rights under the Equality Act · Working with arthritis: UK employment rights · Is arthritis a disability?

Should you tell your employer?

You do not have to tell your employer about your arthritis. But your employer's duty to make adjustments generally applies only when they know, or could reasonably be expected to know, about your condition. Telling them often opens the door to practical help.

It can help to plan what you say: a short, plain explanation of your condition, how it affects your work on good and bad days, and two or three changes that would make the biggest difference. Keep it factual and focused on solutions. Follow up in writing so there is a record.

Read more: Should you tell your employer about your arthritis? · Talking to your employer about RA

Reasonable adjustments that often help

Adjustments are changes to the job, the workplace or working patterns. What is reasonable depends on things like cost, practicality and the size of the organisation. Common examples for arthritis include:

  • A later start or a different shift pattern to allow for morning stiffness.
  • Regular short breaks to change position, stretch or rest.
  • An ergonomic chair, desk set-up, keyboard or mouse, or voice-recognition software.
  • A parking space near the entrance, or a desk close to facilities.
  • Working from home on some days, or a phased return after time off.
  • Swapping heavy or repetitive tasks with colleagues.
  • Time off for hospital appointments and infusions.
  • Recording flare-related absence separately from other sickness absence, where your employer agrees.

Read more: Reasonable adjustments that actually help · Desk set-up for workers with arthritis · Standing desk or sitting desk?

Access to Work

Access to Work is a government scheme that can help pay for practical support if your health affects your ability to work. It can cover things like specialist equipment, help with travel to work if you cannot use public transport, and support workers. It is separate from any adjustments your employer should make, and it is not means-tested. You can apply if you are in paid work, about to start a job or self-employed. Northern Ireland runs its own version of the scheme.

Read more: Access to Work: a complete UK guide · Access to Work library note

Flexible working

Employees in England, Scotland and Wales can ask for flexible working from their first day in a job. This might mean different hours, compressed hours, part-time work or working from home. Your employer must consider the request properly and can only refuse for certain business reasons. A flexible working request is separate from a request for reasonable adjustments, and it can help to make clear if you are asking because of your arthritis.

Read more: Flexible working and pacing · Managing arthritis at work

Time off, sick pay and returning to work

If a flare keeps you off work, you can self-certify for the first seven days and then need a fit note from a GP or another eligible healthcare professional. A fit note can say you may be fit for work with changes, such as reduced hours or amended duties, which can make a gradual return easier.

You may be entitled to Statutory Sick Pay, and your contract may offer more. Ask for an occupational health referral if your employer has a service. A phased return, agreed in writing and reviewed regularly, often works better than going straight back to full duties.

Read more: Returning to work after a bad flare · Returning to work with arthritis (FAQ)

Changing role, retraining or stopping work

Sometimes a job stops being a good fit. Before making a big decision, it is worth exploring adjustments, a change of role within the same employer, or retraining. If you do reduce hours or stop work, check what benefits you may be entitled to. Personal Independence Payment is not based on work or income, and Universal Credit may include extra support if your health limits your ability to work.

Read more: Choosing a career that suits arthritis · Universal Credit and limited capability for work · PIP and benefits guide

If things go wrong

If you feel you are being treated unfairly, start by raising it informally and keeping notes of dates, conversations and emails. If that does not work, you can use your employer's grievance procedure. Acas offers free, impartial advice on workplace rights, and the Equality Advisory and Support Service can help with discrimination questions. There are strict time limits for employment tribunal claims, so get advice early.

Related guides

  • Arthritis and work in the UK
  • Disability rights in the workplace
  • Benefits and PIP hub
  • Travelling with arthritis

faqs.q: Is arthritis classed as a disability at work?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Under the Equality Act 2010, arthritis usually counts if it has a substantial and long-term effect on your normal daily activities, judged as if you were not taking treatment. Some conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis, commonly meet this test.

faqs.q: Do I have to tell my employer I have arthritis?
faqs.a: No, it is your choice. However, your employer usually needs to know about your condition before it has to make reasonable adjustments, so telling them can make it easier to get support.

faqs.q: Can my employer refuse reasonable adjustments?
faqs.a: An employer only has to make adjustments that are reasonable, taking into account cost, practicality and effectiveness. If they refuse, ask them to explain why in writing, suggest alternatives, and seek advice from Acas if you think the refusal is unfair.

faqs.q: What does Access to Work pay for?
faqs.a: It can help towards specialist equipment, travel to work if you cannot use public transport, support workers and some other practical costs. It is not means-tested and does not affect other benefits.

faqs.q: Can I get a fit note that lets me work with changes?
faqs.a: Yes. A fit note can say you may be fit for work taking account of advice, such as altered hours, amended duties or workplace adaptations. Your employer then considers whether they can support those changes.

faqs.q: Can I be sacked for time off because of arthritis?
faqs.a: Absence related to a disability should be handled carefully and fairly, and reasonable adjustments to absence policies may be appropriate. Dismissal is not automatically unlawful, but disability discrimination is. Get advice from Acas or an employment adviser early if you are worried.

/guides/travel-with-arthritis.title: Travelling With Arthritis: Plan Ahead and Enjoy the Trip | Living With Arthritis
/guides/travel-with-arthritis.description: Travel with arthritis made easier: packing medicines and biologics, airport and rail assistance, insurance, travel vaccines, pacing long journeys and flares abroad.
/guides/travel-with-arthritis.question: Travelling with arthritis: plan ahead and enjoy the trip
/guides/travel-with-arthritis.answer: With some planning, most people with arthritis can travel comfortably. Carry your medicines in hand luggage with a copy of your prescription, book free assistance at airports and stations, declare your condition on travel insurance, check vaccine advice early if you take immunosuppressants, and build rest into your plans so a long journey does not trigger a flare.
/guides/travel-with-arthritis.about: Travelling with arthritis: plan ahead and enjoy the trip
/guides/travel-with-arthritis.bodyHtml:
Written by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Updated 2026-09-25. Pending clinical review.

Start planning early

A little preparation weeks before you go saves a lot of stress later. Think about how far you can comfortably walk, how long you can sit, and what usually triggers a flare. Then choose destinations, routes and accommodation that fit, rather than hoping for the best.

If you have inflammatory arthritis, let your rheumatology team know about longer trips, especially if you will cross time zones, need vaccines, or will be away when a blood test or injection is due. They can help you plan the timing.

Read more: Travelling with arthritis in the UK and abroad · Arthritis travel tips (FAQ)

Medicines: pack them properly

Keep all essential medicines in your hand luggage in their original packaging, with enough for the whole trip plus a few extra days in case of delays. Carry a copy of your prescription or a letter from your GP or specialist listing your medicines, especially for injections and controlled drugs.

Some biologic injections need to be kept cool. Ask your homecare provider or pharmacist how long your medicine can be kept out of the fridge and whether they can supply a travel cool bag. Airlines usually allow medical sharps and cool packs in the cabin with supporting documents, but rules vary, so check with your airline before you fly.

Different countries have different rules on bringing in some medicines. If you take strong painkillers or other controlled medicines, check the embassy guidance for your destination well ahead.

Read more: Managing medication when you travel · Packing list for travellers with arthritis

Airports, trains and coaches

UK airports provide free assistance for passengers who need help, from getting through security to boarding. Book it through your airline or travel company when you book, or as far in advance as you can. You do not need to use a wheelchair to ask for help with long distances, queues or luggage.

Rail operators in Great Britain run a free Passenger Assist service to help you on and off trains and with luggage, which can be booked in advance. A Disabled Persons Railcard can reduce fares if you are eligible.

On long journeys, move regularly: walk up the aisle when you can, circle your ankles and gently bend your knees while seated, and drink water. An aisle seat makes getting up easier.

Read more: Flying with arthritis: UK airports

Driving

Plan regular breaks to stretch and walk around, as sitting still for long periods can leave joints stiff. Aids such as a swivel seat cushion, a wide key grip or a steering-wheel spinner can help. You must tell the DVLA if your condition affects your ability to drive safely, and it is worth checking what your insurer needs to know too.

Read more: Driving with arthritis in the UK · Blue Badge vs disabled parking

Travel insurance and healthcare abroad

Declare your arthritis and your medicines when you buy travel insurance, even if your condition feels well controlled. Not declaring a pre-existing condition can mean a claim is refused. Some insurers specialise in medical conditions, and comparing quotes is worthwhile.

A UK Global Health Insurance Card (GHIC) gives access to state healthcare in EU countries and some others on the same basis as residents. It is free, but it does not replace travel insurance because it does not cover everything, such as getting you home.

Read more: Insurance cover and arthritis

Vaccines and infections

If you take DMARDs, biologics, JAK inhibitors or steroids, some travel vaccines, particularly live vaccines such as yellow fever, may not be suitable. Get advice from your rheumatology team and a travel clinic at least a couple of months before you go, so there is time to plan.

Take sensible precautions against stomach bugs and other infections, and know what to do if you become unwell while away. Your team may give you specific advice about pausing medicines during an infection. Only follow advice that has come from them.

Sun, heat and cold

Some arthritis medicines, and conditions such as lupus, make skin more sensitive to the sun. Use high-factor sunscreen, cover up and seek shade in the middle of the day. Heat can add to fatigue, so plan quieter afternoons and drink plenty. In cold places, keep joints warm with layers and gloves.

Read more: Hot weather and arthritis · Cold weather and arthritis

Accommodation and pacing your trip

Ask direct questions before you book: are there steps or a lift, how far is it from the entrance to the room, is there a walk-in shower, and how high is the bed? Photos can be misleading, so a quick call or email helps.

Build rest into your itinerary. Alternate busy days with quieter ones, plan the most important activity for your best time of day, and use taxis or hop-on buses to save energy for the things you came for. A small flare kit, with your usual pain relief, a heat or cold pack and supportive footwear, can help you cope if a flare starts.

Read more: Accessible hotel rooms · Pacing techniques for arthritis · Flare action plan

faqs.q: Can I take my arthritis injections on a plane?
faqs.a: Usually yes, in your hand luggage with a letter or prescription from your doctor. Check your airline's rules on sharps and cool packs before you fly, and ask your pharmacist or homecare provider how to keep the medicine at the right temperature.

faqs.q: Do I need to declare arthritis on travel insurance?
faqs.a: Yes. Declare your condition and medicines, even if they are well controlled. Not declaring a pre-existing condition can mean a claim is turned down.

faqs.q: Can I have travel vaccines if I take methotrexate or biologics?
faqs.a: Many vaccines are fine, but some live vaccines may not be suitable. Speak to your rheumatology team and a travel clinic at least a couple of months before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get help at the airport?
faqs.a: Request special assistance through your airline or travel company, ideally when you book. It is free at UK airports and can help with long walks, queues, security and boarding.

faqs.q: What should I do if I have a flare on holiday?
faqs.a: Use the plan you agreed with your team: rest, use your usual pain relief and heat or cold, and pace activities. If you are very unwell, have a high fever, or a single joint becomes suddenly hot, swollen and very painful, seek local medical help promptly.

faqs.q: Should I change my medicine times when crossing time zones?
faqs.a: Ask your rheumatology team or pharmacist before you travel. They can advise how to adjust timing for daily or weekly medicines safely.
